reasoning_note: Infusion pump in ICU initiating FTP to an unapproved external IP is a direct patient safety threat; the NAC quarantine approach preserves EHR connectivity while blocking the anomalous traffic.
Billing user accessing 47 cardiology records after hours with zero precedent is a clear HIPAA concern; disabling the session and forcing MFA re-auth is the right call.
Unauthorized workstation crossing into the medical device VLAN via SMB is a lateral movement indicator; blocking just that source IP preserves biomed access.
LIS using SFTP to an unapproved destination is a strong exfiltration signal but worth checking with Lab IT first before full isolation since blocking only port 22 preserves lab operations.
Destination resolves to a legitimate Baxter update server; just need biomed to confirm the firmware update cycle and add the IP to the approved list.
High-volume DNS from a patient monitor could be malware beacon or firmware loop; the MVE context about 24 beds losing monitoring if isolated makes me cautious to just rate-limit DNS first.
Float pool nurse explanation makes sense for multi-department access at night; just need to verify with the nursing supervisor before dismissing.
New asset on management VLAN doing an ICMP sweep could be legitimate asset discovery but the fact it has no baseline means we need to confirm with IT Ops before deciding.
Saturday RDP to device VLAN from an unlisted IP is unusual but quarterly biomed maintenance is a reasonable explanation; verifying with biomed before taking action.
Destination is an approved clinical partner and the volume is consistent with a full CT series for second opinion; just verify with radiology as a formality.
Unlike the previous PACS alert, this destination is NOT on the approved list and the 4 AM timing is suspicious; blocking outbound to that specific IP while preserving partner connectivity is prudent.
Unauthorized wireless pairing attempt on an active insulin pump is an immediate patient safety emergency; notifying the endocrinology nurse to switch to manual protocol is the top priority.
Service account accessing 312 records at 39 records/min at 1 AM with no scheduled report is almost certainly post-compromise exfiltration; disable the account immediately.
Ventilator using Telnet is a life-safety issue; blocking port 23 at the VLAN ACL without isolating the device protects the patient while containing the threat.
Internal backup to an approved server with anomalous timing is most likely a rescheduled failed backup; verify with IT Ops and monitor EHR performance.
Pharmacy system transferring to an approved AWS backup destination on a weekend is likely a routine rescheduled backup with no patient care risk.
Quarterly self-diagnostic pattern on the Philips monitor matches a prior baseline event from 3 months ago; adding a suppression rule makes sense.
EHR server scanning all internal subnets including clinical device VLANs is active intrusion; network isolation via emergency VLAN policy is the correct response without powering off.
Physician accessing their own patient panel via authorized VPN after hours is completely normal clinical workflow.
Nurse station uploading 1.1 GB externally at 6 MB/s is automated exfiltration; isolate via NAC immediately and provide the nurse a replacement workstation.

q21_note: The MVE enrichment identifies specific devices, wards, patient counts, and concrete safety risks so a nurse or physician would clearly understand what's at stake.
